Inspired by the observation that original splitting operations cause perturbations in the loss function, this variant modifies the splitting operation so that the resulting density after splitting is similar to the density of the Gaussian being split.
Splitting is performed along the longest principal axis, by shifting means by $\pm \alpha \sigma$, where $\alpha$ is a constant (set to 0.3) and $\sigma$ is the size along the splitting axis.
*   **Time Complexity:** Densification is performed periodically (e.g., every 100 iterations), so the overhead is amortized.
*   **When to use:** Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training where high-fidelity reconstruction is required and memory allows for dynamic growth.

*   **When not to use:** Memory-constrained environments (consider Fixed-Pool Relocation) or scenes with significant motion (consider Temporal Densification) [3094-fixed-pool-relocation.md, 9531-temporal-densification.md].
It was designed to address the sparse initialization problem, where a fixed set of Gaussians cannot adequately represent complex scenes.
